t.1.127.1: Then Adhiratha entered the arena, his upper garment slipping off, sweating and trembling, leaning on his staff for support, as though calling out.
t.1.127.2: Seeing him, Karṇa, his head still wet from the consecration, cast aside his bow and, constrained by reverence for his father, bowed his head to him in salutation.
t.1.127.3: Then the charioteer, flustered, covered his feet with the hem of his garment and said "Son!", his heart's wish fulfilled.
t.1.127.4: Then, embracing him and overcome with affection, he sprinkled his head, still wet from the consecration to the kingship of Aṅga, once more, this time with tears.
t.1.127.5: Seeing him and concluding, "This is the son of a sūta," Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava then spoke these words, as if laughing.
t.1.127.7: And you, lowest of men, are not worthy to enjoy the kingdom of Aṅga, just as a dog is not worthy of the sacrificial cake placed near the fire at a sacrifice.
t.1.127.6: You do not deserve death in battle at the hands of Pārtha, son of a sūta! Quickly take up the goad, which befits your family.
t.1.127.8: Thus addressed, Karṇa, his lower lip trembling slightly, sighed deeply and gazed up at the sun, the maker of day, standing in the sky.
t.1.127.9: Then mighty Duryodhana leapt up in anger from that lotus-grove of his brothers, like an elephant frenzied with rut.
t.1.127.10: He said to Bhīmasena of terrible deeds, who stood there: "Vṛkodara, it is not fitting for you to speak such words."
t.1.127.11: Among kṣatriyas, strength is supreme, and even a lowly man of the warrior class is bound to fight. The origins of heroes and of rivers, as they say, are hard to know.
t.1.127.13: The blessed god Guha, who is wholly made of mystery, is said to be the son of Agni, the son of the Kṛttikās, the son of Rudra, and also the son of Gaṅgā.
t.1.127.12: Fire, by which the whole world of moving and unmoving things is pervaded, arose from water; and from the bone of Dadhīca was made the thunderbolt, the slayer of the Dānavas.
t.1.127.14: Those who were born of kṣatriya women and became brāhmaṇas are also renowned; the Ācārya was born from a pitcher, and the teacher Kṛpa from a clump of reeds. And how your own birth came about, that too has been learned by the kings.
t.1.127.15: How could a doe give birth to a tiger, one born with earrings and armour, marked with divine signs, resembling the sun?
t.1.127.16: This lord of men deserves the kingship of the whole earth, not merely the kingdom of Aṅga, by this might of his arms and with me as one who follows his command.
t.1.127.18: Then from the whole arena there arose a great uproar of "hā, hā!", mingled with cries of "well done!", and the sun went down to its setting.
t.1.127.17: Or whatever man does not accept this deed of mine, let him mount his chariot, or stand on foot, and bend his bow.
t.1.127.19: Then, O king, Duryodhana took Karṇa by the hand and, his way lit by the fire of torches, departed from that arena.
t.1.127.20: And the Pāṇḍavas, together with Droṇa and with Kṛpa, O lord of the people, all accompanied by Bhīṣma, went each to his own dwelling.
t.1.127.21: Some among the people cried "Arjuna!", some "Karṇa!", O Bhārata, and some "Duryodhana!"; speaking thus, they then departed.
t.1.127.23: Then, O king, having found Karṇa, Duryodhana's fear that had arisen on account of Arjuna quickly vanished.
t.1.127.22: And when Kuntī recognized her son, the lord of Aṅga, revealed by his divine marks, her hidden joy grew out of love.
t.1.127.24: And that hero, who had toiled hard at the practice of weapons, addressed Suyodhana with the greatest courtesy. Then even Yudhiṣṭhira came to think that there is no archer on earth equal to Karṇa.
